applicability.rationale: Patients were individually assigned after initial medical examination by minimization to treatment or control in an explicitly parallel-group study.

results.relation_rationale: This selects the reported between-group follow-up workability result, the first-named abstract outcome, without declaring it primary. The body gives 29/45 versus 14/49 able to work (64% versus 28%), whereas the abstract gives control 29%; counts agree. Workability includes school and seeking work, so actual full-time employment alone (17 versus 10) would be a narrower competing construct and is not selected. Baseline-to-follow-up change and sick-leave days are separate results. The target preserves the paper's 4-month timing after graduation, not 4 months after randomization. Reported analysis is narrower than all randomized patients through postassignment exclusion and nonreturn. Counts are retained as source quantities without adding a computed effect, confidence interval, or statistic label. Follow-up ascertainment details and the precise allocation of the stated tests to the endpoint contrast remain unclear.

reported.analysis_population: 45 treated program completers who returned at follow-up and 49 returning controls, out of 55 and 51 randomized. Two treatment nonstarters and seven dropouts excluded, including two who could be contacted; one graduate and two controls could not be reached.

results.requested_outcome: Ability to work at 4-month follow-up (first-named outcome in the abstract; no primary outcome is designated)

comparison_groups.assignment: 3-week full-time multidisciplinary functional restoration with behavioral support; after graduation, 6 hours weekly follow-up training for 3 weeks.
No treatment by the study center; permitted to seek treatment elsewhere.

target.intended_analysis_population: All randomized participants in the comparison groups
target.intended_effect_measure: Between-group comparison of ability-to-work proportions at follow-up

measurement.method: Ability to work (workability: having a job, being in school, or seeking work) assessed at the follow-up examination.
measurement.metric: Ability to work at 4-month follow-up (first-named outcome in the abstract; no primary outcome is designated)

target.outcome_definition: Ability to work at 4-month follow-up (first-named outcome in the abstract; no primary outcome is designated)

time_point_or_window.description: Reported 4-month follow-up: first Monday after 122 days after treatment graduation; controls matched at randomization for the same initial-examination-to-follow-up interval.

answers.justification: Participants received a conspicuous 39-hour/week multidisciplinary program versus no center treatment, and disclosed assignment to the examining physician in some cases. Participant awareness is established.

Providers delivered active group exercise, work simulation and behavioral sessions only to assigned treatment participants; the intervention could not be delivered without knowing assignment. Physician assessor blinding is a separate protection.

Nonstarting and discontinuation arose from illness, pain, difficulty tolerating the program or its smoking rule, and nonappearance. These can occur outside a trial. Seeking outside care was explicitly allowed for controls. The examined conduct provides no strong reason that recruitment or trial personnel caused an inconsistent intervention departure; probably no is justified without claiming perfect adherence.
unknowns: Other unreported deviations and their causes remain unknown.

bases.stopping_rationale: Read full report, treatment/control methods and nonstarter/dropout reasons. No other source or applicable protocol is captured; further lexical searching would not establish unreported trial-context causes.
bases.unresolved_premise: Completeness of deviation reporting is uncertain.

answers.justification: The 45-person treatment analysis is restricted to completers returning at follow-up; two nonstarters and seven dropouts are expressly excluded, including two contactable patients. This is a naive completion-based restriction, not simply an analysis omitting missing outcomes. It is inappropriate for the all-randomized assignment effect.
unknowns: Which of the contacted excluded patients had ascertained workability is unknown; contact alone does not prove outcome observation.

answers.justification: Nine nonstarters/dropouts among 55 assigned to treatment were excluded; seven dropouts were on sick leave at entry and several stopped for increased pain or difficulty. Selecting program completers can select better workability prognosis. These treatment-specific exclusions are large enough relative to the 29/45 versus 14/49 contrast for a substantial impact to be plausible; unknown excluded outcomes prevent an exact impact or direction claim.
unknowns: Excluded workability outcomes and exact bias magnitude are unknown.

answers.justification: The operational definition specifies job, school or seeking work and reports those categories for both arms at examination. This can capture changes in the approved workability construct; no unsuitable instrument or insensitive range is identified. Its broad definition is not itself evidence that the measuring method is inappropriate.
unknowns: How employment, enrollment and seeking work were verified is not reported.

answers.justification: Both groups were examined by the same physician, using the same reported workability definition at matched follow-up intervals. Workability is a status at that visit, not a passively detected event whose ascertainment depends on extra treatment visits. Differential data-collection methods are not suggested by these procedures.
unknowns: Detailed verification procedures by arm are unavailable.

answers.justification: The examining physician's blinding was expressly broken in about 10% of cases, equally across groups, during follow-up. Thus awareness occurred for some assessments. The source does not specify whether workability was independently verified or directly participant-reported; if the latter, unblinded participants also contribute assessment.
unknowns: Workability-specific assessor role and timing of disclosure relative to workability classification are unknown.

answers.justification: Employment and school status are comparatively concrete, but seeking work may require reporting or judgment. With no described independent verification, knowledge of treatment could affect reporting or classification of that component in partially unblinded assessments. This concerns measurement, not genuine changes in employment or job-seeking caused by treatment.
unknowns: Verification and classification discretion for seeking work are unknown.

counterevidence.implication: Attempted physician blinding with balanced breaches provides reassurance and limits an inference of likely biased assessment.

answers.justification: Some awareness and a potentially susceptible seeking-work component establish possibility, but not likely material influence. Most assessments retained physician blinding, breaches were balanced, and most positive cases were employed or in school. The report does not establish participant reporting versus external verification or altered classifications, leaving both a reassuring and an influential mechanism plausible.
unknowns: The actual source of workability data, verification, assessor expectations and consequences of disclosure are unresolved.

bases.stopping_rationale: Read the full report and reread the blinding and workability sections. Only one source is captured; these sections specify no verification or disclosure-related assessment changes.
bases.unresolved_premise: Whether knowledge likely influenced workability assessment remains unresolved.

answers.justification: Workability is reported for 45/55 treated and 49/51 controls. Seven of nine treatment nonstarters/dropouts could not be contacted, plus one graduate and two controls could not be reached. Thus genuinely unavailable outcomes, independently of deliberate exclusions, are plausibly large enough to change this dichotomous contrast materially. The two contacted excluded patients may or may not have supplied workability; contact is not counted as observation.

answers.justification: Follow-up loss is concentrated in the treatment group: seven uncontactable nonstarters/dropouts plus one graduate, versus two controls. The treatment discontinuation reasons include increased back pain, illness and inability to tolerate the program, with all seven dropouts initially on sick leave. Their combination with disproportionate loss supports a probable relation between unavailable four-month workability and its true value. This remains inference, not proof that every lost participant was unable to work.
unknowns: Which health-related dropouts were contactable and the actual outcomes of those lost are unresolved.

The results are based on data collected at a fol-
low-up examination at 4 months (the first Monday
after 122 days after graduation). Each patient in the
control group was matched at randomization with

Return to work
One of the major goals of the project was to
prepare patients physically and psychologically to go
back to work. "Workability" was defined as having a
job, being in school, or seeking work.
At the 4-month follow-up, 29 (64%) of the 45
treated patients were able to work, compared with
12 (27%) at baseline; in the control group, 14
(28%) of the 49 patients were able to work at the
time of the 4-month follow-up, compared with 8
(16%) at baseline. The difference between the two
groups was significant (P < .001); the differences in
the before and after values in the two groups were
also significant (P < .001 by Fisher-Irwin test). Of
the 29 patients able to work in the treated group, 17
had full-time jobs, seven were unemployed but seek-
ing work, and five were in school. Of the patients in
the treated group who could not work, six were
receiving social pensions and the rest were still on
sick leave. In the control group, 10 of the 14 pa-
tients able to work were working full-time, three
were unemployed but seeking work, and one was in
school. Eight persons in this group were receiving
social pensions and the rest were on sick leave.

O B J E C T I V E
The aim of this study was to determine whether a
3-week, full-time, multidisciplinary program would
affect the return-to-work rate, the number of days of
sick leave used, the number of contacts with health
care providers, pain and disability levels, and iso-
metric back-muscle endurance in patients with
chronic low back pain.
M E T H O D S
This parallel-group study was prospective and ob-
server-blinded. After an initial medical examination,
patients were randomly assigned to a treatment group
or a control group according to the minimization prin-
ciple'5 (a means of achieving an even distribution ac-
cording to sex, age, pain and function scores,36 days of
sick leave, and smoking status in the two groups).
Patients
The study included 106 patients referred to the
Copenhagen Back Center between May 1991 and
May 1992. Subjects had to be 18 to 59 years in age,
read and write Danish, have had at least 6 months
of disabling low back trouble, and have a threat-
ened job situation owing to back problems (most
were on sick leave or did not have a job). Most of

the program: one was strongly addicted to mor-
phine, one could not accept the restrictions on
smoking (which was only allowed outdoors), one
felt the program was too difficult, one was found to
have a neurologic disease, and three had increased
back pain they could not accept. All the dropouts
were on sick leave when they entered the program
and did not differ from the graduates in any of the
measured characteristics.
The project was blinded in that the physician
who saw the patients for the initial examination and
the 4-month follow-up did not know which group
each patient was in. The same physician saw all the
patients in both groups throughout the study. The
blinding was broken in about 10% of the cases,
equally distributed between the two groups, when
patients disclosed this information during the fol-
low-up examination.
Treatment
Our program was a modification of the functional
restoration programs described earlier by Mayer31 and
Hazard.20 The concept is described in detail else-
where.3' On the first day, the patients underwent
various tests. Physical tests included dynamic and
isometric endurance, lifting capacity, walking and
running 400 meters, and standing and sitting toler-
ance. The psychological tests included the Millon
Behavioral Health Inventory, the Million Pain Ana-
log Scale, the Symptom Check List 90-R, the Thera-
peutic Alexithymia Scale (TAS), and the Vanderbilt
Coping Questionnaire. A structured psychological
interview was also carried out the first day.
Each patient participated for 39 hours per week
for 3 successive weeks. The daily schedule is shown
in Table 2. The aerobics class included training in
cardiovascular fitness, muscular endurance, coordi-
nation, and stretching. This was followed by pro-
gressive strength and endurance training for all ma-
jor muscle groups, using air-moderated machines
and other training equipment. Occupational ther-
apy consisted of simulated work situations, includ-
ing lifting, pulling, pushing, sitting and standing
workplaces, garden work, and kitchen work. Bio-
feedback was used in some of the sitting work situ-
ations.
The psychological treatment had a behavioral
approach; patients were urged to take greater re-
sponsibility for coping with pain, set realistic per-
sonal goals, change the negative sensation of pain
into a more positive way of living, and give them-

In the daily stretching classes, patients worked on
all major muscle groups. Classes in spinal anatomy
and pathology addressed each patient's condition
and the topics of sexuality, pain, hobbies, nutrition,
and medication. In a 3-hour job-analysis course, pa-
tients learned how to write an application and re-
sumé, find out about job possibilities, and evaluate
advertisements in light of their own abilities and
skills. Recreation consisted of different games and
physical training, such as ball games, walking, run-
ning, and swimming.
All training was carried out in groups of seven
patients. Every Monday, two or three new patients
started the program, and every Friday two or three
patients "graduated." This group structure is essen-
tial, as the program is especially difficult during the
first week. Patients in their third week inspire the
"first-weekers" to endure and encourage them to
continue. This also gives the "third-weekers" a re-
sponsibility and authority in relation to the begin-
ners, which in turn increases self-confidence.
After graduating, patients underwent a follow-up
program of 6 hours of psychological, physical, and
ergonomie training, as described above, once a week
for 3 weeks.
The control group
Patients randomized to the control group after
the medical examination were not treated by us.
They could go anywhere else for treatment, and as
such they represent the "spontaneous" progress of
patients with chronic back pain in Denmark.

Ongoing technological
development has opened
many new doors in the
treatment system, lead-

For many years, the
most frequent treatments

short-term and passive
ones such as manipula-

Because ordinary treatment is not sufficient in
patients with chronic low back pain, several years
ago a new, more active approach was tried that
features intensive physical training. Results showed
that one must exceed the pain threshold and "over-
come oneself' in training intensity.19"21 Not even 2
hours a week of intensive training for a month seem
adequate,19 at least not for hard-working men.22
However, very often, we cannot find an organic
explanation for disabling low back pain.23"2' Com-
plaints of chronic back pain often correlate poorly
with apparent pathology18,26 or with measured
physical capacities and behaviors.27"30 This obser-
vation suggests we ought not only to focus on the
physical part of the pain, but to consider the prob-
lem as a biopsychosocial complex, all parts of
which need to be addressed in treatment. In the
United States, Mayer et al" first proved that in-
tensive multidisciplinary intervention could get
patients back to work, a finding corroborated by
Hazard et al20 and-in a modified program--by
Sachs et al.32 However, modified programs in Nor-
way and Finland failed to get people back to
work.33,34 To our knowledge, no randomized, ob-
server-blinded study has ever been conducted to
test such an intensive multidisciplinary program
for this very expensive, complex problem.
